title: How to Have the Screen Conversation by Age
excerpt: The screen conversation is not one talk. It is a different conversation at five, at ten, at fifteen, and the version that works changes as fast as the child does.
body:
Parents tend to treat screens as a single fight to be won once, usually by setting a rule and defending it. But the child at five who needs a hand pulled off the tablet is not the child at fifteen who carries the entire internet in a back pocket. The conversation has to grow up alongside the kid, or it stops being a conversation and becomes a war of attrition you will eventually lose.

I did not get this right. I set rules I could not hold and gave speeches my sons stopped hearing. What follows is what I wish I had understood earlier, sorted by the age you are actually parenting.

## The early years: you are the limit

From roughly three to eight, the child has no internal brake, and you should not pretend otherwise. This is the season of external structure. Screens live in shared spaces. Time is finite and predictable. You decide, and you do not negotiate it like a hostage situation.

The conversation here is mostly about naming. "Screens are fun, and they are designed to be hard to stop. That is why we turn it off, and it is also why turning it off feels hard." You are teaching a young child that the pull they feel is real, has a cause, and can be resisted. You are also modeling it. A parent scrolling through dinner has already lost the argument before it starts. I have lost it that way more than once.

## The middle years: the why begins

From roughly nine to twelve, the child starts asking why, and "because I said so" curdles into resentment if it is your only answer. This is the season to give reasons and let them be questioned.

Talk about what the device is doing to attention, to sleep, to the way comparison creeps in. Be honest that companies build these things to be hard to put down and that this is not an accident. Twelve-year-olds can handle the truth that they are being engineered, and they tend to respect a parent who tells it to them straight.

This is also the age to start the conversation about what they will see that they did not go looking for. They will encounter cruelty and pornography and despair on the other side of a screen, often before they are ready. Tell them now: when you see something that scares or shames you, come to me, and I will not be angry. The point is to be the safe place before they need one.

## The teen years: from control to coaching

By thirteen and up, the phone is usually in their hand, and the question shifts. You are no longer the wall. You are the coach. A teenager who is controlled but never taught becomes an adult with no internal compass and a sudden, total freedom. That is the worst possible outcome, and rigid control quietly produces it.

The conversation here is about formation, not just restriction. Talk about who they are becoming in the hours they scroll. Ask what an account makes them feel, and whether they want to feel that. Set limits still, but set them with them, out loud, with reasons they can argue. Galatians warns against being mastered by anything. Frame it that way: not "the phone is bad," but "is anything mastering you, and how would you know?"

## What stays constant

Across every age, three things hold.

First, your own phone is the loudest sermon you preach. Children calibrate to what you do, not what you say.

Second, the goal is self-governance, not lifelong surveillance. Every year you should be transferring a little more of the controls from your hands to theirs, on purpose, with conversation.

Third, keep the door open. The worst screen damage happens in secret, to children who believe a parent will explode. Be the harbor, even when what they confess makes your stomach drop.

## This week

Name the age you are actually parenting and have the version of the conversation that fits it. For a young child, narrate one turn-off out loud. For a middle child, give one real reason behind one real rule. For a teenager, ask one genuine question about how a screen makes them feel, and listen without fixing it. Then look at your own usage for a single day and let what you find correct you before you correct anyone else.
